cases.title: The Missing Mango Truck
cases.location: Vashi APMC Fruit Market, Navi Mumbai · 4:55 AM

character.name: Seth Jamnadas Khatri
character.quote: Twelve trucks of Ratnagiri Hapus, Inspector! Do you know what one crate is worth in April?
facts: Biggest mango trader in the market

story: Peak mango season. The air at Vashi smells of straw, diesel and Alphonso.

Seth Jamnadas swears twelve trucks left Ratnagiri last night, 400 crates each. The gate guard wrote every arrival in his register. Somewhere between the Konkan ghats and the mandi, one truck simply… vanished.
Chief Inspector Fatima Qureshi drops the register on your desk. "Your first case, rookie. No guesswork. Let the data talk."

briefing.title: Variables, print, lists, loops & if
points: A variable is a labelled box: crates = 400 stores 400 under the name crates.
print() shows values in the console. Separate several things with commas.
A list keeps many values in order: ["A", "B", "C"]. len(list) counts them.
A for loop visits every item of a list, one by one. Lines inside it are indented by 4 spaces.
if / else makes decisions. == compares, in / not in checks membership.

Multiplication in Python is *, so total_crates = trucks * crates_each.

closing: Truck MH08 HT 4632 is found parked behind a dhaba near Panvel, GPS switched off. Driver Anwar Ali is drinking his fourth cutting chai.
The cargo bay is empty. It was always empty - the 400 crates were only 'loaded' on paper.
"A man paid me to take a long tea break," the driver mumbles. "Cash. He said: the Accountant sends his regards."
Seth Jamnadas thanks you loudly and files his insurance claim the same afternoon. Case closed… for now.

cases.title: The Fake Review Shop
cases.location: Lamington Road electronics bazaar, Mumbai · 11:20 AM

character.name: Prof. Dinesh Bhatia
character.quote: 4.9 stars, they said. The TV died before the India-Pakistan match even started!
facts: Bought a 32-inch TV from Sharma Electronics online

story: Sharma Electronics has the best rating on Lamington Road. Suspiciously the best.
Prof. Bhatia's TV gave up in two days. When he read the reviews again, he noticed they all sounded… the same. "Best product ever!!!" Over and over.
You pull every review from the shop's page. Time to separate real customers from the bots.

briefing.title: Strings, dictionaries & functions
points: A string is text. .lower() makes it lowercase, .strip() trims spaces, and "ever" in text checks if a phrase appears.
A dictionary maps keys to values: {"ravi": 3}. Read with d["ravi"]; d.get(k, 0) gives 0 if the key is missing - perfect for counting.
A function packages logic you can reuse: def name(input): … return answer.
Data from a CSV file arrives as text, so "5" is not 5. Convert with int().

print(len(reviews), "reviews loaded. First one:")
print(reviews[0])

phrase_count = 0
for r in reviews:
    text = r["text"]
    # make text lowercase, then check for the phrase

steps.solution:
import csv

reviews = list(csv.DictReader(open("case2_reviews.csv", encoding="utf-8")))

phrase_count = 0
for r in reviews:
    text = r["text"]
    if "best product ever" in text.lower():
        phrase_count += 1

print("Reviews with the phrase:", phrase_count)
hints: Some bots SHOUT it in capitals. Compare against text.lower(), not text.
Inside the loop: if "best product ever" in text.lower(): then phrase_count += 1.

Shortcut for the biggest: top_reviewer = max(reviewer_counts, key=reviewer_counts.get). Or loop and keep the best so far.

def is_fake(review):
    stars = int(review["stars"])      # CSV text -> number
    text = review["text"].lower()
    # return True only if both conditions hold
    return False

fake_ids = []
for r in reviews:
    # if is_fake(r), add r["review_id"] to fake_ids
    pass

hints: Combine two conditions with and: return stars == 5 and "best product ever" in text.

closing: All 18 fake reviews were posted on the same day from three accounts registered to one phone number.
The 'digital marketing agency' behind them charged ₹5 per review. Its invoices were paid by an account named only 'A.'
Sharma Electronics' rating drops to 2.1 overnight. Prof. Bhatia gets his refund - and a new TV for the World Cup.
Someone is funding small frauds all over the city. You pin a new card on the board: THE ACCOUNTANT?

cases.title: The Railway Ticket Racket
cases.location: CSMT reservation office, Mumbai · 10:00:00 AM sharp

character.name: Albert D'Souza
character.quote: Tatkal opens at ten. By ten-oh-oh-twenty, Rajdhani is full. No human types that fast, men!

story: Every morning at 10:00 sharp, Tatkal booking opens - and every morning honest passengers stare at WAITLIST.
Mr. D'Souza has pulled the booking log for one day's trains. Each row is one ticket: who booked it, through which agent, and how many seconds after the window opened.
Lists and loops won't cut it for hundreds of rows. Time to meet your new partner: pandas.

briefing.title: Pandas DataFrames: load, look, filter, sort
points: pandas gives you a DataFrame - an Excel sheet inside Python. pd.read_csv("file.csv") loads one.
df.head() shows the first rows, df.shape is (rows, columns), len(df) is the row count.
df["fare"] picks a column. df[df["fare"] > 1500] keeps only rows where the condition is True.
Combine conditions with & (and) / | (or), each in brackets: df[(a) & (b)].
df.sort_values("col") sorts; df["col"].value_counts() counts each value, biggest first.
Tip: if your last line is just a value, the console shows it as a table - no print needed.
briefing.example:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "train": ["Rajdhani", "Duronto", "Shatabdi", "Garib Rath"],
    "fare":  [2550, 1900, 1200, 900],
    "quota": ["Tatkal", "General", "Tatkal", "General"],
})
print(df.shape)
print(df[(df["fare"] > 1000) & (df["quota"] == "Tatkal")])
df.sort_values("fare")

closing: Agent AG-4471 runs 'Lucky Travels' out of a one-room office in Kurla: three laptops, one illegal auto-fill bot, booking in under 2 seconds.
Each ticket was resold at three times the fare to desperate families.
In a drawer, a ledger of monthly 'software licence' payments - all to the same account. Initial: 'A.'
Mr. D'Souza makes his 9:15 local on time. Tatkal is fair again. Your evidence board is getting crowded.

cases.title: The Power Theft Grid
cases.location: City Power Board, Ward Office · 9:40 PM, during a blackout

character.name: Er. Meenakshi Iyer
character.quote: We pump the power in, the meters say it never arrived. Electricity doesn't evaporate, Inspector.

story: Three blackouts this week. The transformers are overloaded, but the bills say people are using less than ever.
Somewhere, someone has hooked a cable straight onto the line. Er. Iyer hands you three months of meter readings and the substation supply log.
Warning: the readings are messy. Meter readers spelled area names five different ways, and some meters were never read.

briefing.title: Cleaning data, missing values & groupby
points: Missing values show up as NaN. df["col"].isna().sum() counts them; df.dropna(subset=["col"]) removes those rows.
Text columns have string tools under .str: df["area"].str.strip().str.title() trims spaces and fixes capitals.
df["area"].nunique() counts distinct values - great for spotting messy spellings.
groupby = split, compute, combine: df.groupby("area")["units"].sum() gives one total per area.
Two Series with the same labels can be combined directly: (a - b) / a * 100 lines them up by label.
briefing.example:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "area":  ["Powai", "powai ", "Juhu", " JUHU", "Juhu"],
    "units": [120, None, 300, 150, 90],
})
print("Missing:", df["units"].isna().sum(), "| Spellings:", df["area"].nunique())

df["area"] = df["area"].str.strip().str.title()
df = df.dropna(subset=["units"])
df.groupby("area")["units"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"])

closing: A night raid in Lotus Colony. Behind a shuttered godown: a thick illegal cable hooked onto the main line.
Inside, forty humming freezers - an unlicensed cold storage, stacked to the roof with mango crates.
The godown's lease is in the name of a company you've seen before on a ledger: 'J. Holdings'.
The lights come back on across the ward. Er. Iyer nods. "Electricity doesn't evaporate. Told you."

cases.title: The Cricket Betting Ring
cases.location: Mumbai Monsoon League final, Shivaji Park · 11:58 PM

character.name: Coach Daisy Fernandes
character.quote: Three dropped catches and a run-out a child could avoid. In a FINAL. Somebody sold this match.

story: The Bandra Blasters cruised through the league, then collapsed in the final. The crowd at Shivaji Park went silent.
Cyber Cell seized phone records from a number linked to a known bookie den. You also have the team rosters and the match schedule.
Bookies call at night, when nobody is watching. Let's see who was awake.

briefing.title: Dates, joins, pivots & charts
points: pd.to_datetime(df["col"]) turns text into real dates; then .dt.hour, .dt.date, .dt.day_name() unlock the parts.
merge joins two tables on matching values: a.merge(b, left_on="to_number", right_on="phone") - like VLOOKUP, but better.
pivot_table reshapes data into a grid: rows from one column, columns from another, cells aggregated.
matplotlib draws charts. series.plot(kind="bar") is the quickest way - the chart appears in the console.
briefing.example:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

calls = pd.DataFrame({"to": ["A", "B", "A", "A"],
                      "time": ["2026-08-01 01:15", "2026-08-01 14:00",
                               "2026-08-02 02:40", "2026-08-02 03:05"]})
people = pd.DataFrame({"phone": ["A", "B"], "name": ["Asha", "Sana"]})

calls["time"] = pd.to_datetime(calls["time"])
calls["hour"] = calls["time"].dt.hour
both = calls.merge(people, left_on="to", right_on="phone")
print(both)
both["name"].value_counts().plot(kind="bar", title="Calls per person")
plt.show()

closing: Rocky Malhotra confesses in the dressing room. ₹15 lakh to drop catches in the final, paid through a bookie on +91 98200 13579.
The bookie talks fast once the handcuffs click. He was just the collector, he says. The money went upstream - to 'the Accountant', who never shows his face.
"He always pays in round sums," the bookie adds. "Big ones. At night."
Big transfers. At night. You finally know where to look: the money itself.

cases.title: The Final Heist

character.name: Kaveri Menon
character.quote: Nine hundred transfers in a month. One of them is your Accountant. I just can't see him in the crowd.
facts: Amounts are stored as messy text

story: Every case has whispered the same name: the Accountant. Fake trucks, fake reviews, ticket bots, stolen power, fixed matches - all of it paid upstream.
Kaveri Menon gives you thirty days of transfers and the account register. The amounts are written like humans write them: ₹3,943.09, Rs. 41,000.
No tip-off this time. You'll have to let the numbers tell you who doesn't belong.

briefing.title: Putting it together + NumPy anomaly detection
points: Text money like "₹3,943.09" must become numbers: remove symbols with .str.replace("₹", "", regex=False), then .astype(float).
NumPy does fast maths on whole arrays: arr.mean(), arr.std(), np.abs().
A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the average: z = (x - mean) / std.
Values with |z| > 3 are very rare in normal data (about 0.3%) - classic anomalies.
Then use everything you know: filter, merge, value_counts.
briefing.example:
import numpy as np

amounts = np.array([500, 620, 480, 550, 9000, 510])
z = (amounts - amounts.mean()) / amounts.std()
print(np.round(z, 2))
print("Odd one out:", amounts[np.abs(z) > 2])

steps.title: Count the real money
steps.task: Load case6_transactions.csv into tx. The amount column is text like ₹3,943.09 or Rs. 150. Clean it into a float column (still called amount) and print the total.
steps.starter:
import pandas as pd

steps.solution:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

tx = pd.read_csv("case6_transactions.csv")

tx["amount"] = (tx["amount"]
                .str.replace("₹", "", regex=False)
                .str.replace("Rs.", "", regex=False)
                .str.replace(",", "", regex=False)
                .str.strip()
                .astype(float))

print("Total moved: ₹", tx["amount"].sum())
hints: Chain three .str.replace(old, "", regex=False) calls - one each for "₹", "Rs." and ",".
Finish with .str.strip().astype(float) to remove spaces and convert.
